reasons: The repo has no pyproject.toml, requirements file, or other tools/*.py. A third-party CLI library would be the first dependency, and it would need packaging and pinning.
One maintainer plus years of upkeep favors zero dependencies. argparse is in the standard library, so it can't break on a version bump, and it follows the Python 3.11 release cycle.
Three subcommands is well within argparse's built-in support through add_subparsers.

Strongest case against A is that click and typer need less boilerplate and give nicer help. For three subcommands the saving is a few dozen lines. It doesn't outweigh a permanent dependency. Typer also depends on click, so it adds a chain of dependencies.
If the tool outgrows argparse later, moving to click is a small, local rewrite of one file.

evidence.claim: Repo has no dependency manifest and no existing tools/*.py, so there is no established third-party stack to match (Glob for pyproject.toml, requirements*.txt, setup.py, setup.cfg, tools/*.py returned nothing)
argparse supports subcommands natively via ArgumentParser.add_subparsers. I'm citing this from memory of the official docs and didn't fetch the page.

risks: Typer's and click's current release status and Python 3.11 compatibility were not checked.
The user may already prefer click or typer elsewhere. The brief lists no files, so I can't confirm.
argparse needs more manual code for features such as shell completion or rich help, if those are wanted later.
would_change_if: The repo already depends on click or typer, or the tool is expected to grow to many nested subcommands with completion and rich help.
